problem: 3D object-centric representation learners (uORF, ObSuRF, and similar slot + NeRF methods) fix the number of slots per scene and render every slot, so compute grows with the number of objects. They also decompose each scene independently, so no category-level knowledge is shared across scenes. As a result they only work on simple synthetic scenes (CLEVR-like) and do not transfer to complex indoor or real scenes, or to downstream embodied tasks.
motivation: Object-centric, geometry-aware representations should transfer well to tasks like object navigation and depth reasoning. Existing 2D methods rely only on color cues, and 3D methods do not scale. The driving observation is that a dictionary of object codes shared across scenes has to capture recurring visual and geometric patterns to reconstruct novel views well. Localizing a single code per point also keeps rendering cost constant regardless of scene complexity.
key_idea: Learn a shared, growable codebook of categorical object codes. Each projected scene point is assigned one code (via STE nearest-neighbor), perturbed into an instance code, and decoded by a conditional NeRF to reconstruct novel views. The resulting encoder+codebook is then used as a frozen visual representation for segmentation, depth ordering and ObjectNav.
insight: Discretizing per-point features into a finite shared codebook, supervised only by novel-view reconstruction, pushes the model to group objects by both geometry and appearance (e.g., differently textured couches and floors share codes). This representation transfers better to navigation than contrastive or CLIP features: RoboTHOR ObjectNav SR 50.1 vs EmbCLIP 47.0 and Video MoCo 43.9. The ablation (Table 4, ProcTHOR ARI) shows the intra-code variation module matters most: .182 → .284 with a fixed 25 codes, and .295 with learned codebook size. Learning the codebook size gives only a moderate gain (.182 → .197 alone). A tuned fixed size of 80 codes also reaches .295, so the learned size mainly saves hyper-parameter search. Assigning one code per point is what makes rendering cost independent of object count, which helps most on cluttered scenes: NYU hard ARI .139 vs ObSuRF .092.
method: Image encoding + camera projection: a CNN (modified ResNet34 for segmentation, ResNet50 for navigation) encodes the input frame into a spatial feature map. Each 3D point of the novel view is projected into the input frame with the relative camera pose, and the feature of the patch containing it is selected.

Codebook assignment: the point feature is assigned to its nearest code by argmax over softmax(-||l_i - f||_2). Gradients reach the encoder and codebook through a softmax relaxation in the backward pass (straight-through estimator).

Differentiable codebook growth: code i is gated by T(sigmoid(s - i^2/λ), 1/2), a binarized step function trained with STE. The learnable score s is added to the loss as a penalty, and k+1 codes are kept so s gets gradients. This acts as a discrete Gaussian prior P(k)=exp(-k^2/λ); new codes are initialized from N(0,1).

Intra-code variation module: a 3-layer conv net G takes [categorical code, feature] and outputs a perturbation normalized to norm ε. The perturbation is added to the code to form an instance code close to its category.

Conditional NeRF decoder: an MLP (3 layers, hidden size 512) conditioned on instance code, position and view direction predicts (color, density). Volume rendering (near 0.4, far 5.5) reconstructs the novel view under an L2 pixel loss plus s. Frame pairs are sampled within a 5-frame sliding window of agent videos.

Downstream use: segmentation labels each pixel with its nearest code. Depth ordering combines code masks with depth estimated from rendered transmittance (pixelNeRF-style). For ObjectNav, the frozen encoder+codebook produces instance codes per image region, which feed an EmbCLIP-style GRU actor-critic trained with DD-PPO for 200M steps.

The PointNav dataset/split (Gibson vs MP3D) and episode set are not specified. Also reported but not listed above: NYU Depth hard subset ARI .139 and Matterport3D segmentation ARI .237. Ablations on ProcTHOR ARI (NRC base .182, +learned #codes .197, +variation .284, both .295) and a fixed-codebook-size sweep (best .295 at 80 codes) are also given.
results: On RoboTHOR ObjectNav (test), the frozen NRC representation reaches SR 50.1 / SPL .239. This beats EmbCLIP (47.0 / .200), Video MoCo (43.9 / .184), ObSuRF (38.9 / .167), ImageNet pretraining (33.4 / .150) and uORF (31.3 / .146), all under the same DD-PPO 200M-step policy training. For unsupervised segmentation, NRC improves ARI to .295 on ProcTHOR and .182 on NYU Depth (vs ObSuRF .228 / .141, about 29% relative), while roughly matching ObSuRF on CLEVR-3D (.977 vs .978). Depth-ordering accuracy rises to 23.8% (vs 18.3% ObSuRF), and on Habitat PointNav NRC gets SR .96 / SPL .85 vs ImageNet pretraining .94 / .82.
limitations: Requires camera poses (relative pose between frames) for novel-view reconstruction training, which most images and videos lack. It also assumes static scenes.
NeRF sampling remains compute- and memory-intensive. Choosing corresponding frame pairs is ill-posed under large viewpoint changes (the paper uses a 5-frame sliding window).

Navigation evaluation is limited: one ObjectNav benchmark (RoboTHOR) with a single policy architecture, plus an under-specified Habitat PointNav experiment with no split details. Absolute SPL remains low, and the segmentation benchmark ignores small objects (top-20 classes only).
